The Black–Scholes Formula

Black–ScholesProbabilityAlgebra
Game: One formula gives the fair price of an option. Change the stock, the strike, the time and how jumpy the stock is, and see what moves the price and what doesn't.
How to play: Move the sliders. Press Simulate to check the formula against thousands of random futures.

The call against the stock price; red: the tangent, whose slope is delta. Dashed: the payoff.

Look for the math

Solving the heat equation of the previous page and changing back to dollars gives the Black–Scholes formula for a call:

C = S·N(d1) − K e−rT·N(d2)
d1 = (ln(S/K) + (r + σ²/2)T) / (σ√T),   d2 = d1 − σ√T

Here N is the area under the standard bell curve.

Two pieces

N(d1) is the delta: the number of shares in the hedge, the slope of the red tangent. N(d2) is the risk-neutral chance that the call is used. So the second piece is the strike, paid with that chance and discounted to today. A put is priced the same way, and the two are tied by put–call parity, C − P = S − K e−rT. Owning a call and selling a put is the same as owning the stock with a debt of K due at T.

The Greeks

The table lists the formula's slopes, the Greeks. Delta is the change per dollar of the stock. Gamma is how fast delta itself changes, which is how often a hedge must be adjusted. Vega is the change per point of volatility, theta per day that passes, and rho per point of interest. Volatility always adds value: it widens the spread of outcomes, but the payoff can never go below zero.

Where is μ?

The stock's own growth rate is nowhere in the formula, because the hedge cancelled it. Simulate shows this. Average the payoff over thousands of end prices grown at the bank's rate, and you land on the formula. Grow them at the stock's own rate instead, and you get a different, wrong price. The logic test checked the textbook values ($10.45 call, $5.57 put), parity in 54 cases, every Greek against the price's slope, and 400,000 simulated end prices.

Set the strike far above the stock and raise the volatility. Why does a call that will probably expire worthless gain value?
